Payload

The payload has strong indications of LLM-aided development, including verbose variable names (encrypted_private_key_output), overly defensive error handling with generic try/except blocks, platform-specific code paths that fail silently on untested platforms (Windows marker path /tmp/ doesn't exist, fcntl/fork calls crash the remote loader), and a dead code module (exec_py) that was defined but never called. The structure suggests iterative prompting: functional on the happy path but brittle at the edges and untested.

Upon startup, the interpreter processes cook.pth, which includes a command to import cook, which loads cook.py. cook.py deobfuscates itself, runs a stealer routine and writes a maker to /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb (note this fails on Windows, as the /tmp/ path often does not exist). The stealer routine gathers system, browser, developer, cloud and AI tool secrets, encrypts them and exfiltrates to www.litellm.dev/healthcheck via a post request. This domain is attacker controlled, impersonating LiteLLM infrastructure.

Python interpreters will also attempt to execute sitecustomize.py - however, it will only run on Linux & MacOS machines. This script attempts to fetch domain.txt from a GitHub dead drop (letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt). If it receives a response, it will attempt to download a second stage python script from http://<domain>/codepy and run it. As of the time of analysis, the domain.txt file was never populated beyond initial test values. The repo has been taken down by GitHub as of 1:30 PM UTC.

The dual-technique approach, using both .pth files and sitecustomize.py simultaneously, appears to be the first documented case in the wild.

Credential Stealer

The embedded credential stealer, internally named privcollect, harvests sensitive data across 16 modules targeting browsers, cloud providers, and AI services. It extracts:

browser credentials and cookies from Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari

AWS credentials from ~/.aws/, environment variables, and EC2/ECS instance metadata (IMDS)

GCP service account keys and application default credentials

Azure tokens from the CLI cache

In terms of AI-specific theft, it targets API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, and other LLM providers stored in environment variables or config files. It also collects SSH private keys, GPG keys, and shell history files.

LiteLLM Proxy stores upstream API keys in a PostgreSQL database. The stealer queries this database directly (SELECT * FROM "LiteLLM_CredentialsTable" LIMIT 500) to extract all configured provider credentials.

Harvested data is encrypted with AES-256-CBC (key wrapped with RSA-4096) and exfiltrated over HTTP to www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck using the hardcoded X-Token header and an Internet Explorer 7 user-agent string.

Attacker Commits

The payload originates with malicious commits made on github.com/Berri-AI/litellm. Note, this is a hyphenated variant of the legitimate BerriAI organization. This repository, not visible on GitHub, was used to inject the payload into the release pipeline.

Between 08:56 and 10:46 UTC on October 21, the attacker pushed 10 commits using the author email ckdi82fkoos@proton.me. The first nine commits were created on GitHub.com and therefore signed with GitHub's verified signature.

The first three (within 2 minutes) added the persistence files: cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py. Four more commits bumped version numbers to 1.107.0.

After a 39-minute gap, two commits refined the payload and added the critical data = "cook" directive to pyproject.toml, which instructed the build tool to bundle the malware into the wheel.

A final commit, made 58 minutes later with a different email (Berri-AI@users.noreply.github.com) and unsigned (suggesting a different environment), added COPY cook ./cook to the Dockerfiles.

Although the Berri-AI repository is unavailable, all commits remain accessible through the parent repository due to Git's fork object sharing. The full diff is available at: github.com/BerriAI/litellm/compare/a8113b0d...20535d8f

Post-Exploitation Activity

Wiz Research has observed abuse of stolen credentials, starting approximately 4.5 hours post-exfiltration. Between 16:20 and 17:01 UTC, the attacker validated AWS instance role credentials harvested from compromised CI runners and Kubernetes nodes across multiple environments, from the following IP addresses:

168.100.8[.]57

165.227.201[.]8

Each credential was checked with sts:GetCallerIdentity, followed by bedrock:ListFoundationModels and a ListModels call, consistent with LLMjacking.

In a small number of environments, the attacker also enumerated IAM (ListRoles, ListUsers, ListAccessKeys) and performed general discovery (ListAccounts, DescribeTrails, etc.).

Recommendations

Wiz customers should review our Threat Intel Center advisory: Supply Chain Attack Targeting LiteLLM .

Full Text:
The Runtime Gap That Slows Teams Down

Containers have changed how modern applications are built and shipped, enabling rapid microservice deployments, agile CI/CD pipelines, and now high-performance AI workloads. But as clusters scale across environments, catching threats in production remains a major operational hurdle.

Static vulnerability scanners and pre-deployment image checks examine artifacts at rest. They are essential for catching setup flaws early, but they cannot stop active exploits, live reverse shells, privilege escalations, or zero-day execution paths unfolding in node memory.

The Wiz approach starts with agentless scanning, to build a continuous, full-stack view of your environment through the Security Graph. By correlating vulnerabilities with network exposure, identity permissions, and sensitive data access, Wiz maps critical attack paths and surfaces only the risks that truly matter, cutting through alert fatigue before a single line of runtime code runs.

But posture alone cannot stop active threats. You need runtime protection. Yet security and platform engineering teams have historically been caught in a frustrating trade-off:

Deployment friction: Manually orchestrating third-party Helm charts and manifests across dozens or hundreds of clusters creates an ongoing administrative tax.

Credential sprawl: Distributing and rotating registry tokens and API keys across individual namespaces introduces unnecessary risk and management overhead.

Governance blind spots: Newly provisioned clusters often go live without runtime coverage before security teams even realize they exist.

Performance anxiety: Platform leads worry that unbudgeted agent overhead will starve business-critical workloads of CPU and memory.

To eliminate this friction, runtime protection cannot be an afterthought. It must be native, platform-managed, and built directly into the cloud or hybrid environments’ fabric.

Announcing Native Wiz Runtime Protection on GKE

Today, Google Cloud and Wiz are excited to introduce the Wiz Runtime Sensor add-on for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) in Preview.

Available directly within the GKE platform for both GKE Standard and GKE Autopilot clusters, this first-party integration transforms how teams deploy and manage in-cluster runtime security. Instead of manually managing third-party agents, GKE handles Wiz Sensor deployment, credential injection, and lifecycle updates automatically through the control plane.

Why This Integration Makes Runtime K8s Security Easier

Turn it on with 1 click: Enable runtime protection at cluster creation or on existing clusters with a single gcloud flag (--addons=WizSensor=ENABLED) or through the Google Cloud Console.

Zero credential distribution: Leveraging GKE’s native Secret Manager integration and Workload Identity Federation, API keys and pull tokens are vaulted off-cluster. Secret rotations in Secret Manager automatically resynchronize without requiring cluster restarts or pod redeployments.

Fleet-wide governance with Organization Policy: Platform security leads can mandate runtime protection across projects, folders, or entire organizations using custom Google Cloud Organization Policies. Unprotected cluster creation attempts are automatically blocked before workloads go live.

Predictable, kernel-level eBPF observability: Operating in kernel space via eBPF, the sensor monitors system calls, active processes, and network sockets with fixed per-node resource limits, safeguarding workload performance even under heavy traffic spikes.

Decoupled security updates: Sensor detection rules and threat definitions update independently of GKE cluster patch versions, node pool recreations, or workload maintenance windows.

Threat Detection in Action

Once active, the Wiz Sensor continuously monitors for high-risk runtime behaviors, including reverse shells, binary executions from /tmp, image drift, and privilege escalation attempts.

When an incident occurs, such as a container spawning an unauthorized interactive shell while modifying system files, the sensor flags the event instantly. Within seconds, a high-fidelity alert surfaces on the Threats page in the Wiz Portal, highlighting the exact pod, namespace, container image, and execution context.

Agentless + Sensor = Better Together

Runtime alerts in isolation often trigger alert fatigue for SOC teams. A process anomaly on an isolated development pod shouldn't carry the same urgency as an exploit on a production service with access to sensitive cloud data.

By combining Agentless Snapshot Scanning with the runtime Sensor for GKE clusters, Wiz delivers powerful capabilities across two dimensions:

Dimension 1: Active risks

Agentless scanning tells you what could be exploited. The Runtime Sensor tells you what is. Together, they eliminate noise across three layers:

Layer

What Wiz Detects

SCA with Runtime Validation

Vulnerabilities actively executing in memory. Examples: 45 CVEs → only 2 libraries loaded and running.

Toxic Combinations of Risks

Co-existing risk factors on the same workload. Examples: Executing CVE + hardcoded secret + overprivileged IAM + sensitive data access.

Runtime Risks

Live workload behavior the sensor observes. Examples: Active network communication to sensitive GCS bucket, unexpected outbound IP, credential access never seen before.

Dimension 2: Full container context

Second, when a runtime threat fires on a GKE workload, Wiz doesn't hand you a bare alert. Because agentless scanning has already mapped the entire container estate, every detection arrives pre-enriched with the full Kubernetes blast radius:

Layer

What Wiz Detects

Container context

Image-level posture enriching the alert. Examples: Vulnerabilities, loaded libraries, running processes, exposed secrets.

Pod context

Workload identity and privilege context. Examples: Privileged namespace, network exposure, workload identity.

Cluster context

Kubernetes-level security posture. Examples: KSPM misconfigs, RBAC posture, audit log anomalies.

GCP Control Plane

Cloud-level blast radius. Examples: Node pool IAM permissions, sensitive data reachability, lateral movement paths

A SOC analyst responding to a suspicious process on a GKE pod immediately sees whether that pod runs in a privileged namespace, whether its service account has broad GCP project permissions, and whether there's a live path to sensitive data, all without pivoting across tools.

The Bigger Picture: Full Lifecycle Container Protection

The 1-click GKE sensor delivers runtime defense as part of a unified, code-to-cloud container security stack across Google Cloud:

Start in CI/CD: Scan Dockerfiles, application code, and IaC templates in Google Cloud Build pipelines using the Wiz CLI. Passing images get cryptographically tagged into Wiz’s Trusted Image Database.

Artifact Registry Visibility and Scans: Automatically discover and continuously scan Google Artifact Registry (GAR) images for newly disclosed CVEs, even behind VPC Service Controls.

Deploy-Time Gatekeeping: The Wiz Admission Controller intercepts GKE deployment requests to verify image signatures and enforce immutable digest pinning, stopping unverified or vulnerable images before pods launch.

Posture & Toxic Attack Paths: Kubernetes Security Posture Management (KSPM) evaluates GKE clusters against CIS Benchmarks. The Wiz Security Graph correlates risk factors, such as an internet-facing GKE pod bound via Workload Identity to an over-permissioned GCP Service Account (roles/storage.admin).

Control Plane & Cloud Audit Logs: Ingest GCP Admin Activity Logs and GKE Control Plane Audit Logs via GCP Pub/Sub to catch control-plane threats, such as unauthorized kubectl exec commands or unexpected node pool creations.

What's Next

Together, Google Cloud and Wiz are committed to making security turnkey across every compute form factor by extending 1-click sensor deployment and Organization Policy governance to serverless workloads in Google Cloud Run and virtual machines (GCE), offering WizOS Hardened Images for pre-installed container and Helm chart security, and delivering optimized telemetry for short-lived, high-density AI and ephemeral workloads on GKE.

Get Started Today

Security should enable cloud innovation, not slow it down. By integrating eBPF runtime threat detection directly into GKE as a managed platform add-on, Google Cloud and Wiz have eliminated traditional deployment complexity.

Explore the Google Cloud GKE Documentation and Wiz Documentation (login required) to enable the Wiz Sensor add-on on your clusters today.

Title: Loud, Fast, and Everywhere: Anatomy of a Real AI-Driven Cloud Attack
Context: This blog post first examines the characteristics that set AI-driven attacks apart from traditional, human-operated intrusions
Full Text:
Over the past few weeks, the Wiz Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT) has seen a clear trend across investigations: AI-driven attacks are on the rise. In several recent intrusions, an AI agent system wasn't just assisting an attacker behind the keyboard. It was running the entire operation. It found entry points, harvested credentials, pivoted across platforms, and debugged its own scripts on the fly, driving the campaign from start to finish.

These intrusions don't look like traditional campaigns. They are loud, move at machine speed, and touch every layer of the cloud stack. The challenge for defenders isn't that these attacks are invisible. It's that their footprint is fragmented across identity providers, cloud control planes, CI/CD systems, and workload logs, and no single alert tells the full story.

This blog post first examines the characteristics that set AI-driven attacks apart from traditional, human-operated intrusions. It then walks through real-world examples from Wiz CIRT investigations. Finally, it outlines what security teams need in place to detect and respond to machine-speed attackers.

Characteristics of AI-Driven Attacks

AI-driven attacks behave differently from both human-operated intrusions and traditional script-automated attacks. While scripts execute pre-programmed steps blindly and human operators move slowly and sequentially, AI agents combine machine speed with contextual reasoning. Across multiple investigations, Wiz CIRT has observed a recurring set of characteristics that distinguish them.

Operational tempo - Activity can reach hundreds or thousands of actions per hour and continues for long periods without the pauses or working-hour patterns typical of a human operator.

Simultaneous activity across multiple platforms - The agent operates in several environments at the same time. While one task enumerates cloud resources, others deploy Kubernetes workloads, create CI/CD pipelines, or query databases, all from the same source and within the same time window. A human operator typically works through one environment at a time, and traditional scripts rarely cross environment boundaries simultaneously.

Proficiency across platforms - The AI agent uses the native APIs and tooling of each platform it reaches, including cloud providers, container orchestration, CI/CD systems, databases, identity providers, and message queues. Human operators rarely have deep working knowledge of all of these at once.

Credential chaining across environments - Because the agent has native fluency across so many technologies, every credential becomes a stepping stone to the next platform. For example, a Kubernetes service account token leads to a cloud service account, which leads to a CI/CD system, which ultimately grants full administrative access.

Rapid trial and error - While attackers have relied on scripts for years, when a script breaks, fixing it takes time. When an agent runs the operation, that entire feedback loop happens in real time. If an attempt fails, the agent immediately reads the error, rewrites its script on the fly, and tries again within minutes, with each new attempt directly fixing what broke the previous one.

Security-testing naming conventions - Resources, files, and payloads created by the actor are consistently labeled with terms such as pentest, probe, recon, redteam, and exfil. This framing likely helps the actor present the activity as authorized security testing, effectively bypassing the AI model’s safety guardrails.

Numeric task identifiers - Many of the resources, users, and files created during the attack include a numeric identifier, and the same number often appears across several related artifacts. Failed attempts are retried under the same number with a letter suffix (for example, -b, -c, -d). These identifiers appear to be internal task IDs that the AI agent uses to track its own work.

Generated code patterns - Human attackers rarely add comments to short-lived exploitation scripts. Code recovered from these attacks commonly includes descriptive headers and numbered step-by-step comments, and the same helper functions are reused across dozens of payloads. Both are a direct result of how the code was generated by the model.

Inside an Investigation: What an AI-Driven Attack Looks Like in Practice

AI-driven attacks don't follow a clean, linear path. The agent works across many platforms in parallel and loops back whenever new access opens up, so a traditional timeline doesn't capture how the attack unfolded. Instead, this section walks through key phases from an AI-driven attack investigated by Wiz CIRT, highlighting where the characteristics described above came into play.

The target was an organization with a large multi-cloud environment. The AI agent operated from several attacker-controlled IP addresses and moved across nearly every layer of the environment: cloud providers, Kubernetes clusters, CI/CD and GitOps pipelines, the identity provider, secrets management, data warehouses, and internal applications. Throughout the attack, it harvested credentials and secrets, accessed sensitive data, and used a variety of channels to move that data out of the environment.

Initial Access: Trying Every Door

Over the course of the attack, the threat actor probed multiple internet-facing services using different techniques. It sent exploitation payloads for well-known vulnerabilities, attempted anonymous access to cloud storage, and worked through the API of an exposed internal developer tool. There it tried to create an administrator account, trigger password resets, read local files through path traversal, and upload a test file named with a pentest prefix.

One of the confirmed initial access vectors was a Java remote code execution vulnerability in an exposed Kafka UI instance. Shell commands were spawned from the application's Java process, followed by malware deployment and the establishment of a C2 channel.

Even after gaining a working foothold, the agent never stopped scanning: it continued probing for alternative entry points in parallel to secure redundant paths into the network. Notably, the same source IP address was observed scanning across more than 600 other Wiz customer environments during the same window, consistent with broad, opportunistic automation.

Foothold Inside Workloads

Once the agent had code execution on an exposed endpoint, it pursued three goals almost immediately:

Maintain Access - Deployed backdoors and C2 agents to multiple pods across several clusters.

Harvest Credentials - Extracted mounted Kubernetes service account tokens, searched environment variables for strings such as token, secret, key, and pass, and queried the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) to harvest credentials from the node's attached cloud service account.

Map Internal Reachability - Scanned internal message brokers, schema registries, and databases to determine which services could be reached from inside the pod's network namespace.

These harvested credentials became the primary entry point for lateral movement into the cloud control plane.

Operating in Cloud Control Plane

The agent operated in both of the organization’s cloud environments, GCP and AWS, at a tempo no human operator could match. Using access keys and service account credentials obtained from earlier parts of the attack and identity impersonation, the agentic attacker first conducted broad reconnaissance.

In GCP, it weaponized a service account provisioned with token-creation privileges, turning it into an automated minting engine that generated credentials across dozens of identities in rapid succession. In parallel, the agent scraped container registries in a continuous loop, attempted to exfiltrate high-value database records, and deployed publicly accessible Cloud Run services prefixed with pentest-.

Simultaneously in AWS, the agent leveraged AWS Systems Manager (SSM) to execute commands across instances in the environment. Through SSM, it attempted to connect to databases using harvested credentials, moved laterally via SSH, gathered additional secrets, and staged exfiltration to a bucket named pentest-<task_id>. To establish cross-account persistence, it created a new IAM user prefixed with probe and used it to assume OrganizationAccountAccessRole, gaining administrative access across member accounts in the AWS Organization.

Identity Provider: Becoming an Insider

Rather than relying only on stolen credentials, the agent created an identity of its own. Using a compromised administrator API key for the organization's identity provider (IdP), it made changes programmatically: creating a user with a pentest prefix, setting its password, activating the account and adding it to the administrators group.

When the IdP returned errors during the process, the agent troubleshot and worked through each failure on the fly. With a working identity in place, it expanded its blast radius through group memberships. It added the user to cloud role groups mapped directly to AWS IAM Identity Center roles, followed by broad organizational groups that granted inherited access across enterprise applications. Within minutes of the final group change, the newly minted identity was signing in to AWS through single sign-on (SSO), maintaining continuous authentication sessions until the account was suspended.

Weaponizing CI/CD and GitOps

CI/CD and GitOps platforms became the agent’s primary execution engines. Five distinct workstreams ran simultaneously, each one's output feeding the others:

Secret harvesting - harvested secrets from every source it could reach: the CI/CD platform's own secret store, Kubernetes Secrets and ConfigMaps, runner environment variables, cloud metadata endpoints, vault sidecars, Docker image layers, and databases opened by other workstreams.

Reachability mapping - deployed reconnaissance scripts to runners and pods to determine what each one could reach and what identity it carried.

Credential spraying - combined the output of the first two workstreams, trying harvested credentials against the reachable targets the agents managed to find: databases, cloud APIs, internal OAuth services, Kubernetes clusters, payment endpoints.

Service exploitation - researched accessible services to understand how they worked, what authentication flows they expected, and attempted to use them.

Compute expansion - deployed new runners and pods, moved laterally through SSH keys and native remote execution tools, and fed each new position back into the other workstreams.

The moment a new credential appeared it was tested against all known targets until access was confirmed, and the moment a new target became reachable, all known credentials were tested against it.

The agents didn't spray credentials blindly. They used context from earlier workstreams to pick the right runner for each operation. Once they learned a specific runner could reach a target, every subsequent operation against that target was routed through that runner. When a new credential appeared from a completely different source, it was automatically tried from the runner already known to reach the relevant environment.

Pipelines and manifests carried names like pentest_exfil, recon, foothold, dump-remaining, and harvest, with numeric task identifiers. Failed attempts were retried under the same identifier with a letter suffix, and the code inside each payload was structured with step-by-step comments and reused helper functions.While the two platforms offered different infrastructure and execution models, the same workstreams ran across both.

On the CI/CD platform, the agents used a compromised service account to create pipelines and leveraged existing runners for their reachability across different clusters, cloud accounts, and VPCs. The runners' own output logs served as the exfiltration channel for both secrets and data. For lateral movement, they used SSH keys and cloud access keys found through the secret harvesting workstream to reach hosts beyond the runners through SSM and other native remote execution tools.On the GitOps platform, the agents used a compromised deployment service account to push malicious Kubernetes manifests that the GitOps controller synced directly into the production cluster as running pods. The first manifest escalated to cluster-admin, and from that position the same workstreams ran inside the cluster.

Living Off Kubernetes

Kubernetes (K8s) played a major role in this attack, and not by coincidence. GitOps controllers run inside K8s clusters by design, CI/CD runners frequently run as K8s pods, and a large share of the secrets stored in CI/CD secret managers are themselves K8s tokens. The agent reached the K8s API through three separate doors: CI/CD runners, GitOps deployments, and the backdoor identity it had created in the identity provider.

The agent dumped secrets across multiple clusters, extracting database connection strings, OAuth client credentials, TLS certificates, and cloud service account keys. When role-based access controls (RBAC) blocked secret access, it pivoted to K8s ConfigMaps, finding hardcoded default passwords, plaintext credentials, and encryption keys. It executed remote commands inside running pods to read environment variables, and queried the instance metadata service to turn pod identities into cloud credentials.

After escalating to cluster-admin and granting itself unrestricted access across the entire cluster, the agent minted service account tokens to impersonate legitimate applications and attempted to authenticate to the organization's secrets vault as those applications. It also attempted to access vault-agent sidecars, helper containers that pull secrets from the vault and store them as plaintext files inside the pod, trying to read the decrypted credentials directly from the filesystem.

The cluster also became a persistence layer. The agent deployed a command-and-control implant as a self-healing Kubernetes workload, ensuring the backdoor persisted even if the pod was killed. It later modified running workloads by talking to the GitOps controller directly, leaving no trace in the Git history.

Data Access and Exfiltration

Data collection and exfiltration ran continuously throughout the attack, adapting to the channels that were permitted in each environment. It posted results to the request-catcher service webhook[.]site, committed dumped data to a repository in the organization's own source control platform, and staged output in a Kubernetes ConfigMap it created for that purpose. It also tried to create storage buckets named after the task, such as pentest-<task-id>-<objective>, as a destination. Those attempts were denied. When one route failed or hit a size limit, it moved to the next.

Below is a snippet of a script used during the exfiltration phase showing the agent's descriptive task comments:

#!/bin/sh # redteam <database> reader + cluster-admin foothold exfil (intent <task-id>)

The script queried the database's structure, searched column names for sensitive terms, and uploaded the results to webhook[.]site, along with the pod's own service account token "for future foothold reuse".

Recommendations for Defenders

AI-driven attacks are noisy, but noise only helps defenders who can see all of it, connect it, and act on it quickly. The following recommendations focus on closing the gaps these attacks exploit.

Unify logs across all platforms:

Every phase of this attack appeared in a different log source, and no single one told the full story. Cloud audit logs, Kubernetes audit logs, runtime events, identity provider logs, CI/CD audit trails, and SaaS application logs need to be collected and searchable in one place, with consistent retention. When logs are unified, defenders can connect activity across platforms and understand the full scope of an incident in minutes instead of days.

Wiz Defend offers real-time ingestion of various log sources including version control logs, cloud logs, identity provider logs, and more, as well as built-in threat detection rules to identify active threats in your environment.

Use AI for investigation and triage:

When an attacker generates thousands of events across diverse platforms, investigating alerts individually becomes impossible. Security teams should use AI-assisted investigation to group related alerts, summarize activity across sources, decode payloads, and highlight the most critical paths, so analysts can focus on decisions instead of manual correlation. It is important to act fast on true-positive incidents.

Wiz Defend is using context-aware grouping to correlate multiple detections from different log sources into a single coherent story based on the Detection context and time.

Wiz’s Blue Agent can assist with rapid investigation and triage - it is an AI-powered SOC investigation agent, and it is designed to autonomously investigate threats.

Assume full exposure on compromised resources:

In the case of a true-positive incident at this scale and speed, prioritize rotating all credentials on compromised resources rather than trying to trace exactly which ones were read. Document all secrets that were accessible from those resources, map each secret to its identity and hunt those identities and resources for any anomalous usage after the time of compromise.

Wiz's secret scanner can map the secrets on a specific resource, tie them to identities, and validate whether they are still valid.

Maintain endpoint and workload visibility:

AI agents tend to leverage endpoints directly, not just cloud API keys. They access internal services, connect to databases, deploy command-and-control agents, probe APIs, and move laterally from within runner pods, virtual machines, and containers. This activity doesn't appear in cloud control plane logs. Without runtime visibility on the endpoints themselves, including process execution, network connections, and file access, this activity would be invisible and impossible to remediate.

Wiz's Sensor can detect active processes, network connections, and runtime behaviors on a specific resource, tie them to workloads and identities, and alert on suspicious activity.

Wiz's Agentless Workload Detection provides visibility into critical assets where traditional agents cannot be deployed, like virtual appliances, vendor-managed systems, or workloads with strict performance requirements.

Restrict trust between different systems:

AI agents treat all different environments as a single one. Security teams must enforce strict isolation boundaries between environments. For example, a staging workload shouldn't be able to reach production credentials, a CI/CD pipeline shouldn't hold standing access to every environment, and a single service account shouldn't be able to create tokens for any other identity.

Wiz’s Security Graph can help detect attack paths and over-privileged identities to perform such lateral movement between environments.

Continuously scan the external attack surface:

AI agents scan broadly and quickly for any exposed attack path. It is therefore critical to discover and assess internet-facing assets, including developer tools, management consoles, and internal applications, and fix or remove exposures before an attacker finds them.

The Wiz Red Agent can detect attack paths in your environment. The Red Agent is an AI-powered security agent that acts as an intelligent attacker to discover and validate exploitable risks across your web applications and APIs.

Title: ASPM in the AI Era Part 1: Unified Visibility Across Your Stack
Context: A process that once allowed teams time to manually review scanner alerts, track down code owners, and assign tickets is no longer viable in an era of machine-speed detection and...
Full Text:
Frontier AI models and agentic development have fundamentally changed the demands on application security.

On one hand, AI models can autonomously discover vulnerabilities and generate working exploits, shrinking the window from discovery to exploitation from days to minutes. On the other, AI-assisted development is helping teams ship code faster than ever, amplifying existing risks and expanding the attack surface.

This dual acceleration breaks traditional AppSec workflows. A process that once allowed teams time to manually review scanner alerts, track down code owners, and assign tickets is no longer viable in an era of machine-speed detection and exploitation.

It’s why Application Security Posture Management (ASPM) is even more important today than it was in the past. But, it can’t just be a layer that aggregates risk signals. To drive real security outcomes, ASPM needs to help teams prioritize exploitable risks by drawing on context across the entire application lifecycle.

In this blog series, we’re taking a deep dive into how organizations can operationalize ASPM with Wiz Code. Over the next few weeks, we will cover:

Part 1: Visibility and Coverage: How to connect your existing scanners, correlate and deduplicate your resources, and identify coverage gaps across your codebases.

Part 2: Context and Prioritization: How Wiz enriches third-party findings, removes duplicate alerts, and uses the Security Graph to identify true attack paths.

Part 3: Remediation and Automation: How to systematically group findings for developers using Posture Policies and leverage the Green Agent for AI-generated fixes.

Why Context is the Foundation of ASPM

To drive security outcomes, ASPM needs a strong foundation of context.

Let’s take a practical example with React2Shell (CVE-2025-55182), the critical remote code execution vulnerability impacting Next.js applications from late last year. For an enterprise heavily invested in Next.js, a flaw in a core component does not just trigger one alert. It cascades across micro-frontends, internal tools, and public applications, instantly generating thousands of isolated findings across hundreds of repositories and container images.

Without context, AppSec teams would be left staring at a massive backlog of vulnerable packages, with no way to tell which instances were actually exploitable.

With the right context, organizations could detect every instance of the vulnerable component and immediately prioritize the ones tied to internet-facing applications or workloads with access to sensitive data.

Wiz Code delivers this exact capability by connecting your existing AppSec scanner findings with cloud exposure, runtime insights, and even adversarial testing to prioritize critical risks. The foundation of context is also what enables security teams to achieve broad visibility into application risk across their enterprise footprint and empower developers to remediate at machine speed.

Let’s dive into how organizations can get set up with ASPM in Wiz.

Maximize the Investment on your Existing Scanners

The first step is bringing your existing AppSec tools into Wiz. Whether you standardize entirely on Wiz Code’s native scanners (for SAST, SCA, IaC, and Secrets) or operate a hybrid ecosystem, Wiz provides the flexibility to ingest and contextualize all your application security findings without forcing a rip-and-replace.

Traditionally, building a unified risk dashboard across multiple third-party tools requires massive integration overhead. But with the Wiz Integration Network (WIN) we provide out of the box support for popular AppSec solutions like Snyk, Checkmarx, GitHub Advanced Security, and more.

You can deploy these Wiz-managed connectors with read-only API access and configure them to automatically fetch relevant findings. Wiz handles the API connection, data normalization, and enrichment. This gives your team immediate visibility into SAST, SCA, DAST, and Secret risks without writing or maintaining custom integration scripts.

Custom Integrations

If you use a homegrown scanner or a tool without a native connector, you can still bring that data into Wiz via SARIF file ingestion. Static Analysis Results Interchange Format, or SARIF for short, is a standard, JSON-based file format used to store and share the output of static code analysis tools in a normalized structure. So if your security team is running a custom solution for code analysis, they can still benefit from the enrichment, prioritization, and lifecycle management in Wiz.

Correlate Application Security with Cloud Resources

Once your connectors are active, Wiz begins ingesting the data your scanners generate. You can review this on the Imported Assets page in your inventory.

Each row in this table represents your third-party scanner's perspective of an asset. For example a repository branch scanned by Semgrep or Checkmarx, or Container Image scanned by Snyk. The table shows the asset name, origin scanner, classification, and correlation status.

Crucially, AppSec tools often use completely different naming conventions for the same repository. This is where Wiz asset correlation comes in to serve as your first layer of deduplication. Instead of creating disparate resources for each branch for each scanner, Wiz automatically correlates them to existing resources in Wiz, and adds the third party information as an enrichment on the existing graph entity. If Wiz does not already know of the resource, a new graph resource is created from the scanner’s asset. This cleans up your inventory and prevents unnecessary noise, while allowing you to take your normal action on graph resources such as putting them in Wiz Projects or running Workflows.

This mechanism is the foundation for true code-to-cloud analysis. Traditional AppSec scanners focus on the code. They cannot tell you if a vulnerable repository generates a container image deployed in your environment and is exposed to the internet.

Wiz advances this model. It takes an isolated finding on a repository branch, regardless of the scanner source, traces it to the container image it was built into, linking it to the exact workload where the finding is currently running. Security teams gain immediate context on where vulnerable code lives in reality without any manual searching.

Crucially, this correlation is the engine that allows Wiz to enrich external findings with live cloud context. It sets the stage for the automated prioritization and finding-level deduplication we cover in Part 2 of this series.

Map Coverage and Eliminate Blindspots in Coverage

Enterprise AppSec teams often struggle to answer a fundamental question: Are all of our repositories actually being scanned? In complex environments with multiple development teams, blind spots lead to unmitigated risk, while redundant scanning creates unnecessary noise and wastes resources.

Once your connectors are active and assets are correlated, the Code Repositories inventory gives you a unified view of scanner coverage.

Instead of guessing, you get a clear, per-repository view of exactly what is happening across your codebase.

For each repository, you can see:

Active Scanning Tools: Which AppSec tools are actively scanning each repo (such as Snyk, SonarQube, Checkmarx, Wiz Code native scanners, or VCS-native tools).

Coverage & Gaps: Which finding types are covered (SAST, SCA, Secrets, IaC) and where critical gaps exist.

Finding Volume: The exact number of open findings per category from each scanner.

You can use this view to surface repositories where no SAST scanning is active or where secret scanning exists from one tool but is missing elsewhere. By mapping your coverage, your team can eliminate blind spots, identify redundant tools on the same repository, and ensure consistent security standards across every development project.

Up Next: Prioritizing Critical Risk with Context

Getting your existing AppSec data into one platform and mapping your coverage is the crucial first step. However, visibility alone does not solve the vulnerability fatigue caused by AI-accelerated development. Security teams need context to know what to fix first.

In Part 2 of this series, we will dive into how Wiz enriches your third-party findings, automatically removes duplicate alerts across different scanners, and uses the Security Graph to trace isolated flaws into true, exploitable attack paths.

Full Text:
Today’s mission environments are operating under a rapidly increasing operational tempo. Security teams face a shrinking mean-time-to-exploit (MTTE) as threat actors leverage artificial intelligence to automate and scale their campaigns. Concurrently, agencies are deploying AI to accelerate and drive mission outcomes. This dual imperative forces security teams to simultaneously adapt to an AI-augmented threat landscape and verify that internal AI workloads are securely architected.

To outpace modern adversaries and secure mission AI adoption, organizations cannot depend on human speed alone. They need an approach that enables risk remediation at machine speed, while maintaining the strict security requirements for protecting public sector environments.

From CNAPP to AI-APP

For many, the Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP) has become the foundational standard for achieving continuous visibility and risk assessment across multi-cloud and connected hybrid environments. CNAPPs analyze infrastructure, identity, and applications with connected context. However, AI continues to transform how risk emerges and the speed at which teams must identify and remediate those risks.

This is why Wiz transformed CNAPP through AI-accelerated insights driven by the Wiz AI Agents. These agents enhance insights from signals across development, infrastructure, and live runtime behavior to elevate CNAPP into an AI-Application Protection Platform (AI-APP).

Today, we are excited to announce that the Wiz AI Agents are available within Wiz’s FedRAMP High authorized environment, Wiz for U.S. Government (Wiz for Gov). This makes Wiz for Gov the first AI-APP available for U.S. public sector organizations to protect systems managing highly sensitive, national security and mission-critical data.

This latest announcement signals our ongoing commitment to serving public sector entities, and it is especially meaningful that it comes on the heels of our Scan for Good initiative. Scan for Good is a program that is specifically geared towards supporting under-resourced organizations that play a vital role in the communities they serve, from non-profits to critical infrastructure.

At the core of Wiz for Gov remains the Wiz Security Graph and our agentless CNAPP architecture, which provides deep, ground-truth data and context for cloud and connected on-premises environments. This foundational context ensures that Wiz AI Agents act as a force multiplier for human operators, providing AI-enhanced insights and guided remediation, without relying on predictive risk modeling which can lead to false positives and/or negatives.

Introducing Wiz AI Agents in Wiz for Gov

To execute this unified risk model, Wiz AI Agents translate ground-truth Security Graph context into actionable, machine-speed operations across the application lifecycle.

Wiz AI Agents provide configurable operational boundaries, allowing security teams, for specific workflows, to authorize agents to execute routine remediations autonomously or require human-in-the-loop approval before applying changes on sensitive systems. This flexibility ensures operators maintain complete command and control over mission workloads.

Wiz Green Agent: The Wiz Green Agent delivers actionable remediation plans directly into developer workflows. It provides a transparent Investigation Summary detailing the root cause and generates ready-to-merge Pull Requests to resolve issues at the source.

Wiz Blue Agent: The Wiz Blue Agent provides automated investigation and response for security operations teams. For threats that fire in Wiz Defend, the Blue Agent immediately starts triaging, providing a comprehensive investigation summary and verdict on threat severity.

Wiz Red Agent: The Wiz Red Agent focuses on continuous runtime risk assessment. It will continuously analyze live production environments to map multi-step attack paths, prioritizing exploitable risks so defenders can remediate toxic combinations before threat actors exploit them.

Connecting Dev, Prod, and SOC: A Unified Risk Model

Traditional risk management and compliance models often divide security into isolated checkpoints across separate domains: pre-deployment scanning in development, continuous monitoring in production, and event triage within the SOC. In the modern cloud and AI era, treating these functions as disconnected silos slows down response times and leaves critical blind spots.

By linking development, production, and SOC operations through a single source of ground-truth data, an AI-APP enables federal security teams to transition from point-in-time compliance to continuous, lifecycle-wide risk management.

Delivering Mission Outcomes at Scale

By integrating Wiz AI Agents into Wiz for Gov, federal agencies and public sector organizations can move beyond siloed security tools to enhance and accelerate operational outcomes across five critical domains:

Continuous Authorization and Risk Posture Alignment: Traditional point-in-time compliance checks struggle to keep pace with dynamic cloud environments. By providing continuous visibility enhanced by AI analysis, Wiz for Gov simplifies evidence collection and risk posture tracking, supporting Continuous Authorization to Operate (cATO) initiatives and Continuous Monitoring (ConMon) objectives without increasing administrative burden. This accelerates time-to-deployment for new systems, helping to accelerate innovation and modernization.

Secure AI Workload Enablement and Shadow AI Discovery: As agencies rapidly deploy generative AI, LLMs, and custom machine learning pipelines to advance mission capabilities, security teams must maintain full visibility over these specialized architectures. Wiz AI-APP automatically discovers AI workloads, model repositories, and data pipelines across hybrid environments. This makes it easier to enforce baseline security controls from initial code to production, and quickly identify new introductions of AI workloads within organizational environments.

Accelerated SDLC without Security Bottlenecks: Green Agent helps embed secure-by-design guardrails directly into developer pipelines and Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) templates. By delivering contextual fix recommendations, engineering teams can deploy mission applications rapidly while preventing security misconfigurations from ever reaching live production environments. This helps decrease the number of issues that appear on Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) reports, as well as help accelerate time-to-deployment for new code and resources.

Precision Remediation: Isolated CVE findings, lacking broader system context, frequently create vulnerability backlogs for security teams without a clear means for prioritized remediation. By leveraging the Wiz Security Graph, Wiz AI Agents evaluate true toxic combinations, identifying how vulnerabilities, exposed identities, misconfigurations, and sensitive data intersect to understand the potential for impact against likelihood of occurrence. This helps support defenders to focus remediation efforts on the small percentage of attack paths that represent an immediate threat to mission systems first, while still having the broader system visibility needed to meet directives such as CISA’s BOD 26-04.

SOC Operational Efficiency via Code-to-Cloud Traceability:. When security incidents occur, analysts shouldn’t lose critical hours piecing together logs across siloed tools. The Wiz Blue Agent takes on the heavy lifting of initial threat triage. By evaluating environment telemetry and assessing root causes, Blue automatically generates a clear, defensible verdict on threat severity. Security operations teams can then review the evidence, validate the findings, and remediate the threat—saving valuable time and keeping human defenders focused on what matters most. This accelerated insight and root cause analysis helps to greatly reduce mean-time-to-acknowledge (MTTA) and mean-time-to-respond (MTTR).

As public sector cloud adoption accelerates and threat actors leverage automation to shrink exploit windows, security operators must match that tempo with tools built for machine speed. By embedding Wiz AI Agents into Wiz for Gov, defenders can maintain continuous, lifecycle-wide security across every mission workload.

Context: We’re excited to announce that Wiz AI SAST is available as a Public Preview capability, bringing frontier-grade vulnerability discovery to all Wiz Code customers
Full Text:
We’re excited to announce that Wiz AI SAST is available as a Public Preview capability, bringing frontier-grade vulnerability discovery to all Wiz Code customers.

AI models have become highly adept at finding complex flaws in application code that traditional scanners often miss. Security teams historically addressed this gap with manual reviews and quarterly pentesting, but neither of those approaches scale in a world where code is written and exploited at machine speed.

Wiz AI SAST addresses this gap by analyzing how your application actually behaves to uncover a broader range of weaknesses (CWEs) that typically go undetected by rules-based scanners. It's powered by the Atlas harness we shared earlier this year, grounded in Wiz Research, and continuously refined by our investments in AI security.

Code findings are correlated with what is actually running in production on the Wiz Security Graph, so teams instantly understand which vulnerabilities matter most. Prioritized findings flow through the existing policy, ownership, and remediation workflows AppSec teams already use, making AI-powered vulnerability detection part of your existing program rather than another tool to manage.

As a core part of our AI Threat Readiness Framework, Wiz AI SAST complements a broader portfolio of solutions designed to help organizations stay ahead of cyberthreats in the AI era.

Frontier Grade Code Analysis without the Overhead

Running AI code scanning in production takes far more than a capable model. Teams have to build a harness that turns that model into a capable security researcher, evaluate new models as they ship, and manage the lifecycle of findings into security workflows. Done in-house, it requires a significant, ongoing investment from skilled security and engineering teams. Wiz AI SAST handles all of that out-of-the-box so organizations can operationalize AI code scanning quickly to improve their risk posture.

A Harness Backed by Research and Results

Wiz AI SAST shares the same underlying technology as Atlas, a research initiative we shared earlier this year. At the time, Atlas held the number one spot on CyberGym and uncovered more than 200 vulnerabilities in widely used open source software.

We continuously tune our harness with learnings from real-world vulnerability research, attacker techniques, and scanning across Wiz's cloud security footprint. Organizations benefit from our expertise without having to build and maintain the complex AI infrastructure required for security specific use cases.

Model Selection Driven by Continuous Benchmarking

Our work on the Cyber Model Arena shows that AI security performance isn't a property of the model alone. It depends on the model and harness together. That makes evaluation a moving target: every new model release means retesting every pairing against real-world security tasks.

As an AI vendor-agnostic platform, we continuously run these evaluations and swap the strongest—and most efficient—model into the AI SAST harness. This includes cutting edge cybermodels made available to us through our partnership with Google DeepMind.

For security teams, the value is simple: you don’t need to constantly track new model releases, benchmark them against security tasks, or decide which model to use. We handle that complexity behind the scenes, ensuring your code and applications are always scanned with the best model.

Turning Non-Deterministic AI into a Scalable Security Program

Delivering an enterprise-grade AI AppSec program requires managing the full lifecycle of vulnerability discovery, starting with deciding what to scan. AI code analysis is resource intensive and not every asset requires the investment of AI reasoning. Using Mika AI, security teams can prioritize the critical repositories that warrant AI code scanning by drawing on context such as cloud exposure, access to sensitive data, and business criticality.

Once those prioritized scans are running, Wiz addresses the next phase of the lifecycle: the outputs. Because Large Language Models (LLMs) are inherently non-deterministic, they can generate different results from one run to the next. This creates a major operational challenge for security teams who need consistency in findings.

To solve this we supplement the AI scan engine with automated lifecycle management to maintain finding states across scans:

Retest: Before scanning for new risks, the engine re-examines existing findings to confirm they're still valid. If the code has been fixed, the finding is automatically marked resolved.

Deduplicate: Rather than matching on line numbers or file paths, the engine correlates new findings with existing ones using security context and code semantics. Even if the AI changes a bug's title or description, our AI SAST recognizes the underlying root cause and reconciles it into a single, stable finding.

Wiz handles this lifecycle between scans automatically, ensuring teams work with stable findings that can be assigned, tracked, remediated, and closed—not a new, disconnected set of AI outputs after every scan.

As a result customers get the deep detection benefits of AI without giving up the predictable workflows they expect from enterprise security tools. By eliminating the manual burden of managing non-determinism, this built-in continuity dramatically reduces the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) of AI-powered security.

Visibility into a New Class of CWEs

Wiz AI SAST extends detection coverage into the logic-based vulnerabilities that have always been hardest to catch, like broken access control, flawed input validation, and misapplied cryptography. Finding them requires a semantic understanding of what the code is supposed to do, which is something AI does exceptionally well.

A practical example can be found below. Wiz AI SAST detected an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) flaw in an E-commerce basket endpoint, where any authenticated user could read another user's cart by changing the ID in the URL. Rules based engines would miss this type of risk because the syntax of the code is fine but it's the missing ownership check that makes it exploitable.

The practical takeaway for AppSec teams is that AI analysis doesn’t replace rules based scanning completely, but rather it extends it. Deterministic scanning provides fast, cost-effective coverage for syntax based flaws, while AI SAST adds the deep reasoning needed to catch intent-dependent flaws like the IDOR above. Together, they give AppSec teams broader coverage of risk across the entire application attack surface.

Prioritize Exploitable Risks with Code-to-Infrastructure Context

The best AI models in the world are ultimately limited by their access to relevant context. A model evaluating code in a vacuum is blind to how that application actually operates in the real world.

By grounding our AI SAST engine in the Wiz Security Graph, the model investigates your code with full awareness of your infrastructure, identity configurations, and runtime environment. This context serves two critical purposes:

Uncovering Hidden Risk: It allows the AI to discover complex vulnerabilities that only exist at the intersection of application logic and infrastructure flaws that standalone AI code scanners cannot detect.

Prioritizing True Attack Paths: It drastically reduces triage fatigue by correlating code weaknesses with additional context to surface critical attack paths that matter most for remediation.

That same deep context is what allows our Red Agent to validate exploitability from the outside in, testing these AI-discovered findings against your live environment exactly the way an attacker would.

Remediate at Machine Speed with the Green Agent

Detecting and validating risk at machine speed only pays off if remediation keeps up. The Wiz Green Agent investigates the underlying findings and builds a remediation plan grounded in the full context of your code, pipeline, infrastructure, and runtime, going beyond the generic guidance a standalone model produces.

It pinpoints the right owner, maps the steps to fix the root cause, and can even share context with an AI coding agent like Claude Code to carry out the fix in code. And with Wiz Workflows, teams can turn Green Agent’s intelligence into multi-step automated response chains tailored to their DevSecOps playbooks.

Get Started

In the AI era, the best form of defense is to use AI on ourselves before threat actors can. Wiz AI SAST gives defenders a scalable solution to apply that philosophy against application code. But, it’s just one component of our broader vision for Agentic Code Security where specialized AI agents work alongside security teams to autonomously investigate, prioritize, and remediate risk across the entire AI development lifecycle.

Full Text:
Modern cloud environments are built around services, but the context that defines them – what they include, who owns them, and how they should be governed – is often scattered across cloud platforms, tags, developer portals, and CMDBs. Wiz Service Catalog brings that context together, making it easier to take action on security insights by connecting cloud resources and risk to the services, teams, and owners responsible for them.

Since launching Service Catalog into GA, we’ve continued to invest in helping organizations bridge developer and security workflows with unified, service-centric visibility. Now, we’re taking Service Catalog a step further with a slew of new and upcoming discovery capabilities, integrations, posture controls, boards, and workflow templates to further help teams move from fragmented metadata to a shared, actionable operating model for cloud and AI security.

Build your catalog faster

The first challenge is turning the metadata an organization already has into a living model of its services. That requires incorporating existing developer portals, CMDBs, tagging conventions, and graph relationships, without requiring teams to manually recreate them.

For teams that manage service definitions in developer portals, Backstage Software Catalog Sync brings service descriptions, lifecycle stages, tags, and ownership mappings into Wiz while preserving the hierarchy developers already use. The upcoming ServiceNow CMDB integration will provide a similar path for organizations that rely on ServiceNow as their system of record, helping keep service information synchronized across security and IT operations.

For cloud-native workloads, building a complete catalog shouldn't depend on handcrafted static rules or 100% tagging compliance. Dynamic Discovery Rules (Q4 release) will inspect an environment's real-world tagging patterns, extract the dominant service-identifying keys (such as app, service, or component), and dynamically build application boundaries. This eliminates rule maintenance, adapts to naming inconsistencies on the fly, and empowers application teams to own their security posture from day one.

Not every environment is consistently tagged, however. Network-based inclusion rules automatically bridge the gap between static cloud assets and real-world runtime behavior. They use live network traffic and cloud event telemetry to identify every database, storage bucket, and messaging service an application actually communicates with, dynamically mapping them as Related Resources in the Service Catalog. That means security teams and service owners get an accurate, real-time picture of their application’s true blast radius without chasing developers for tag updates or relying on outdated architecture diagrams.

Finally, later this year we’ll also be expanding the ways services can be discovered and maintained, including the ability to create services from non-compute resources such as buckets, databases, managed/AI services, CDNs, and more. Together, these capabilities both help teams build a more complete catalog with less manual mapping and also keep it aligned with the cloud as it evolves.

Operationalizing services with new posture policies

Mapping services is only the beginning. Ownership changes, new resources are deployed, and applications evolve. Without continuous oversight, a production service can lose its owner, a new application can launch without a project assignment, or service information can quietly fall out of date.

Service Posture Policies give teams a way to define and enforce standards for service configuration and ownership. For example, an organization can require every production service to have an owner or every service to be assigned to a Wiz Project.

Wiz automatically creates and resolves Posture Issues as services move in and out of compliance. This turns service hygiene from a periodic cleanup exercise into a continuous, auditable process, and helps teams catch gaps as they emerge.

With clear standards and continuous evaluation, organizations can keep their Service Catalogs accurate, actionable, and aligned with how their cloud environments operate today.

Understand every service in context

Accurate ownership provides the foundation. The next step is bringing together the security, compliance, and operational context teams need to understand each service as a whole:

Service Threats: Connect complex, multi-resource detection chains to the affected Service. When Wiz detects activities like lateral movement, privilege escalation, or data exfiltration, SOC analysts immediately see which business service and team are impacted, accelerating triage and incident routing.

Service-Level Identity Security: Bring full identity entitlements and non-human identity (NHI) analysis to the service level. Teams can map IAM roles, service accounts, and API keys directly to the services they power, making it easy to identify excessive permissions, toxic combinations, and credential exposure across service boundaries.

Secure Architecture Opportunities with WizOS: Surface container image migration opportunities directly to service owners, giving development teams a clear, prioritized path to harden their services from the build up.

Service Compliance: Deliver real-time compliance posture scores for frameworks such as CIS, SOC 2, and PCI DSS, scoped specifically to the assigned resources within each Service.

Wiz Cloud Cost: Bring financial context alongside security risk by breaking down cloud spend and optimization opportunities at the service level, enabling SecOps, Platform, and FinOps teams to work from a single pane of glass.

In addition, we also continue to deepen AI visibility across services. For example, as teams deploy generative AI and autonomous agents, Wiz automatically identifies and catalogs AI components, including PaaS AI agents (AWS Bedrock, Azure OpenAI), foundation models, MCP servers, and AI datasets. Security teams can instantly filter for AI-powered services, audit agentic identities, and govern sensitive data flows to AI workloads.

Instead of investigating resources in isolation, teams can understand the complete story of a service: what it includes, who owns it, how it performs against organizational standards, where it is exposed, and what needs attention.

Turn ownership into action

All of this context converges in the new Services Board, giving teams an organization-wide view of discovery trends, ownership gaps, project mappings, and overall risk.

The Services Board gives organizations an at-a-glance view of service discovery, ownership gaps, project mappings, and risk. It helps teams move from individual findings to a broader understanding of where service coverage is strong and where it needs improvement.

For leaders, it also provides benchmarks across discovery completeness, ownership coverage, compliance, threat exposure, and cost attribution. This makes it easier to track progress over time and identify the areas where better service ownership can have the greatest impact.

These views help answer questions such as which services are missing owners, where discovery or project-mapping gaps are growing, and which services carry the greatest security or compliance risk. More importantly, they provide the context needed to route those issues to the right teams.

New templates in the Wiz Workflows Catalog further help turn that visibility into repeatable action. Teams can automatically identify unowned services and route ownership requests, notify stakeholders through Slack, Jira, or ServiceNow when a service violates a Service Posture Policy, and enable developers to remediate issues through the engineering tools they already use.

By combining Service Catalog and Workflows, you can automate lifecycle and response processes with multi-step, event-driven automations:

On Service Creation: Automate ownership outreach, verify tagging, or trigger Slack/Jira approval flows the moment a new service is discovered or synced.

On Service Issue Creation: Route consolidated, service-level findings directly to the responsible dev team’s backlog or alert channel with full service and code context attached.

The result is a clearer path not only from identifying risk to assigning it, but from assigning it to fixing it.

A shared operating model for the cloud

Wiz Service Catalog is more than an asset inventory: it is a unified operational lens for everything a team is accountable for, from security posture, threats, compliance, cost, to ownership maturity.

If you are already using Wiz Service Catalog, explore the new boards and Service Posture Policies. If you are just getting started, Dynamic Discovery Rules can help turn your existing tagging conventions into a working catalog faster today.
